2027-07-31.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives the weekday readings of the Fourth Saturday of Kaitha and the readings of the commemoration of Saint Ignatius of Loyola; both sets are shown here (verify locally which are read). The calendar's own headings: “Those who have delighted in wickedness will be condemned”; “Woe on unrepentant people”; “Everything for the glory of God”; “A disciple of Jesus must give up everything”. The Latin Church keeps today the memorial of St Ignatius of Loyola, priest.
2027-07-31.verse: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
theo: On the last day of July the Church remembers a soldier who became a saint. Ignatius was born in 1491 in the castle of Loyola in the Basque country of Spain, the youngest of a large family, and was brought up to be a knight, with dreams of fame and glory. In 1521, at the siege of Pamplona, a cannonball broke his leg. During the long months of recovery he asked for novels of chivalry, but the house had only a Life of Christ and a book on the lives of the saints. He read them, and he noticed that when he thought about the saints, he was left joyful and peaceful, whereas his dreams of worldly glory left him dry. That was the beginning of a conversion. He laid down his sword before the altar of Our Lady at Montserrat, lived in prayer in a cave at Manresa, and wrote the notes which became the Spiritual Exercises. As a student in Paris he gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier and Peter Faber, and in 1540 the Pope approved their Society of Jesus. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622. His motto has gone round the world: Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, “for the greater glory of God.”

That motto comes from today's reading from Paul: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” Everything: eating and drinking, work and rest, prayer and the market. Ignatius taught that God can be found in all things and that every action can be offered to him; he built a whole spirituality out of the morning offering of the day. One of his companions, Francis Xavier, came to India in 1542, working first at Goa and then among the fishing communities of the coast of southern India and Travancore; Jesuit schools and colleges have since served many families in Kerala. The Holy Qurbana in our Church shows the same principle in another form: the bread and the wine, ordinary things of the table, are lifted up so that God may be glorified in them.

The Gospel is one of the strongest of Luke. Large crowds travel with Jesus, and he turns and says what no recruiting officer would say. “Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.” In the language of Jesus, “hate” means to put in second place: Matthew has it plainly, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” The family is not despised; but Christ must come first. Then two small parables: a man who wants to build a tower sits down first and counts the cost, and a king going out to war considers whether he has ten thousand men to meet twenty thousand. “So therefore, none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.” Ignatius did precisely that. When he put his sword on the altar of Montserrat, and when he left his family's wealth and a possible career at court, he was not despising the world; he was counting the cost and choosing the better kingdom. His prayer, which is known in many languages as the Suscipe, runs in substance: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding and my entire will; all that I have and possess you have given me, and to you I give it back; give me only your love and your grace, and I am rich enough.

The weekday readings are quieter and harder. In the Gospel, Jesus and the disciples pass the fig tree in the morning and find it “withered away to its roots.” Peter remembers and says, “Rabbi, look!” Jesus answers, not with an explanation but with a call: “Have faith in God.” And he adds the sentence about the mountain: “if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and if you do not doubt in your heart, but believe that what you say will come to pass, it will be done for you. So I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.” The Church has always understood this as a promise that faith and prayer, joined to the will of God, can move what looks immovable. A lame ex-soldier with a handful of friends started a movement that now serves in nearly every country; that is a mountain moved. In Kaitha, the harvest season, we pray in faith for the harvest of the Lord.

Paul's words to the Thessalonians have a darker edge, and they must be read with care. He speaks of “the mystery of lawlessness” that is already at work, of a power of lies, signs and wonders that deceives “those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.” The apostle does not give a timetable; he gives a warning that deception is real, and that the defence against it is the love of truth. A little further on he gives thanks that God chose the Thessalonians “as the first fruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and through belief in the truth.” Ignatius made this into the art of discernment: not every light, not every wonder and not every fervour comes from God, and we must test the spirits and hold to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). A believer in the world of the mobile phone and the news feed, where false things are quickly spread, needs this love of the truth as much as any Thessalonian. Tomorrow we begin August; let us offer to God the whole of the month, and say with Ignatius: for the greater glory of God.
outline: A knight with a broken leg, two books, and a conversion: Ignatius of Loyola.
Point 1 · Everything for the glory of God
Paul's rule and Ignatius's motto; finding God in all things; Francis Xavier in India.
Luke 14: put Christ first; tower and king; give up all; the Suscipe.
Point 3 · Have faith, and love the truth
Mark 11: faith and prayer move mountains; 2 Thessalonians: love the truth and test the spirits.
“Whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.”
live: Each morning this week say a short offering: “Lord, all that I do today, for your glory.” Add one concrete task you will do with special care.
Think of one decision you have been postponing for the sake of Christ, and write down what it would cost and what it would gain.
Before sharing a message or a news item on your phone, ask: is it true, is it kind, does it serve the truth?
Pray daily this week for one specific good intention, with trust that God hears.
fathers: Man is created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul. All other things on the face of the earth are created for man, to help him in the pursuit of the end for which he is created.

Faith is stronger than mountains. The Lord does not say that faith will move you a mountain for show, but that nothing is impossible to those who believe; and the thing that is most impossible, the conversion of a hard heart, is moved by prayer.

Those who love the truth find truth where they find God, because God is truth. Let us not be among those who love the sound of wonders more than the truth; whoever loves the truth does not fear to be corrected.
magis: Before Christ's second coming the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers; the deception of evil and the mystery of iniquity will be unmasked, and only the truth will stand.

In the Gospel Jesus tells the young man who asks what to do: if you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and come, follow me; the commandments are the beginning of the way.
Jesus calls us to pray with faith: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it; prayer of faith is not only words but a disposing of the heart to the will of the Father.
saints: Fourth Saturday of Kaitha. Saint Ignatius of Loyola (about 1491–1556), priest, founder of the Society of Jesus (the Jesuits). In the Latin calendar, his memorial.
Sunday 1 August, the Fifth Sunday of Kaitha (verify locally).

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-31.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you called Ignatius from the battlefield to the service of your kingdom, and taught him to find you in all things. Teach us to do everything for your glory: our work and our rest, our eating and our prayer. Give us the courage to count the cost and to put you before everything, and the faith to ask you for great things. Keep us from deception, and give us a love of the truth that tests every spirit and holds to what is good. Bless the Jesuits and all who teach in the schools and colleges of our land. Take, Lord, and receive our liberty, our memory, our understanding and our will; give us only your love and your grace, and we shall be rich enough. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the bread and the wine are placed before God, and so is our whole day. We offer them for his glory, and he gives himself back to us as food. Ignatius sat before the altar with his sword laid down; so we sit before it with our worries, our work and our plans, and say: Take, Lord, and receive.

quick: Paul to the Thessalonians: the mystery of lawlessness is at work; those who refuse to love the truth are deceived; God chose you through belief in the truth.
Mark: the fig tree withered; Jesus says, “Have faith in God”; believe that what you ask for in prayer will be yours.
Ignatius's readings: do everything for the glory of God; a disciple counts the cost and gives up all.
2027-07-31.action: Offer your whole day to God each morning, saying, “for your glory,” and test one message you receive before you pass it on.
2027-07-31.question: What would I do differently today if everything I did were for the glory of God?
kidsaint: Ignatius was a brave soldier in Spain. A cannonball hurt his leg, and he had to stay in bed for months. He had nothing to read except a book about Jesus and a book about saints. He read them and thought, ‘I want to be a brave soldier for Jesus!’ He started the Jesuits, and his friend Francis Xavier came to India. Ignatius's motto was: for the greater glory of God. Lesson: do even small things for God, and use your mind and your heart for him.
term: Latin for “for the greater glory of God.” It is the motto of Saint Ignatius and the Society of Jesus, and it comes from Paul's rule in 1 Corinthians 10:31: whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. Jesuits often write the letters AMDG at the end of letters and on books and buildings.

family.explain: Saint Ignatius was a soldier who loved to dream about being famous. When he was hurt and in bed, he read about Jesus and the saints, and he decided to work for God. Paul says: whatever you do, do it for God's glory, even eating and playing and studying. Jesus says: have faith in God, and pray; he hears you. So we can offer our whole day to God each morning and ask him for what we need.
family.intention: We pray for all teachers and students in schools and colleges, and for the Jesuits who serve in India.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us do today just for God's glory? What shall we ask God with faith?”

illus: A carpenter near Changanassery (a story told to illustrate the reading) cut, under every table or door that left his shop, three small letters in a hidden place: AMDG. A customer once found them and asked what they meant. ‘For the greater glory of God,’ said the carpenter. ‘A hidden mark?’ asked the customer. ‘Nobody will see it.’ ‘That is the point,’ he replied. ‘God sees it, and the joint I make where nobody will look must be as good as the one in front.’ Later, a builder asked him to put cheaper wood in the back of a cupboard to save money. The carpenter refused, and offered to work a day longer without being paid for it. ‘I could not sign it,’ he said. The cupboard still stands in a house at Kuttanad after two floods.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you call us to follow you and to do everything for your glory. Gather us now, and teach us to find you in all things. Amen.
share: Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). What in my day is hardest to offer to God?
Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost? (Luke 14:28). What would following Christ more fully cost me?
Have faith in God (Mark 11:22). What do I need to ask with more faith?
Test everything; hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). How do I test what I hear and read?
pm.resp: Lord, take and receive; for your greater glory.
interc: For the Church, that she may do all things for the glory of God.
For the Society of Jesus, for teachers and students in our schools and colleges, and for all missionaries.
For those who are deceived by lies and wonders, that they may love the truth.
For those who are struggling with a great decision, that they may count the cost and choose well.
For the month of August, that we may offer every day to God.
pm.close: Father, you gave Saint Ignatius to the Church as a servant of your glory. By his prayers, help us to offer you everything we do, and bring us to your kingdom. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today the Church remembers Saint Ignatius of Loyola. He was a soldier in Spain, about five hundred years ago, who loved to dream about glory. At the siege of Pamplona a cannonball broke his leg, and he lay in bed for months. He wanted to read stories of knights, but the house had only a book on the life of Christ and a book on the lives of the saints. He read them, and slowly his heart changed. He left his sword at the altar of Our Lady, and he began a new life. He founded the Society of Jesus, and one of his first friends, Francis Xavier, came to India.

His motto comes from the second reading: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Do everything: eating, working, studying, resting, praying. Ignatius taught us to find God in all things and to offer the whole day to him. Every morning we can say: Lord, today everything for your glory.

The Gospel is demanding. Jesus says that to follow him we must put him first, even before our family, and give up everything that stands in his way (Luke 14:26, 33). He gives two small parables: a man building a tower first counts the cost, and a king going to war first counts his soldiers (Luke 14:28–32). Ignatius counted the cost. He left the court and the comfort and chose Jesus. His prayer says: “Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding and my entire will.”

The weekday readings give two more lessons. In the Gospel, Jesus says: “Have faith in God” (Mark 11:22). Faith and prayer can move mountains. A lame soldier with a few friends started a movement that now serves in nearly every country. And Saint Paul warns the Thessalonians that deception is real, and that the defence against it is the love of the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:10). We need this love in a world of rumours and false messages. Test everything, and hold fast to what is good.
Tomorrow August begins. Let us offer the month to God, saying with Saint Ignatius: for the greater glory of God. Saint Ignatius, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Saint Ignatius was a soldier whose leg was hurt. In bed he read about Jesus and the saints, and he said, ‘I want to be a soldier for Jesus!’ He started the Jesuits, and his friend Francis Xavier came to India. Ignatius's motto was: for the greater glory of God. Every morning you can say: ‘Jesus, today everything I do is for you.’ Then even brushing your teeth and doing your homework is a prayer!
